summary: This informational document discusses points to consider when designing a solution for identifying flows in MPLS networks. The key application is in-band performance monitoring of MPLS flows. It records considerations rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: An MPLS network labels each packet with the path it should take. To measure how well that path is working, someone has to be able to tell which packets belong to the same flow. This document sets out the choices that have to be made before a way of doing that can be designed.

subtitle: What to weigh before designing a way to tell traffic flows apart inside an MPLS network.

tldr.problem: Measuring the loss and delay of real traffic inside an MPLS network needs the network to say which packets belong together, and the obvious way of injecting test packets does not measure what users actually experience.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists the units a flow could be identified by, the kinds of Label Switched Path where the existing label stack is enough and where it is not, and the constraints any scheme has to respect.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of considerations rather than a protocol: it takes no position on how the identification should be done, and it says the unit of identification and the method are left to the use case.

today: RFC 8372 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the set of considerations for MPLS flow identification rather than a specification of one. It has no IANA considerations, and it deliberately leaves the unit of identification and the method of determining which packets constitute a flow to the application or use case.

sections.title: Why Flows Need Identifying
sections.content:
The document discusses the aspects that need to be considered when developing a solution for MPLS flow identification. The key application that needs this is in-band performance monitoring of MPLS flows when MPLS is used to encapsulate user data packets.

There is a need to identify flows in MPLS networks for various applications, such as determining packet loss and packet delay measurement. A method of loss and delay measurement in MPLS networks was defined in RFC 6374. When used to measure packet loss, that method depends on the use of injected Operations, Administration and Maintenance packets to designate the beginning and the end of the packet group over which loss is being measured. If the misordering of packets from one group relative to the following group, or the misordering of any of the packets being counted relative to the Loss Measurement packet, occurs, then an error occurs in the measurement. That method also did not support different granularities of flow, and did not address a number of multipoint cases in which two or more ingress Label Switching Routers could send packets to one or more destinations.

Because the loss rate in normal operation is very low, and improvements in link and transmission technologies have made it harder to assess packet loss using active measurement with synthetic traffic, operators now need to be able to measure the loss of the actual user data traffic using passive performance measurement methods. Any technique deployed needs to be transparent to the end user, and it needs to be assumed that they will not take any active part in the measurement process. Indeed, it is important that any flow identification technique be invisible to them, and that no remnant of the measurement process leaks into their network.

Additionally, when there are multiple traffic sources, such as in multipoint-to-point and multipoint-to-multipoint environments, there needs to be a method whereby the sink can distinguish between packets from the various sources; that is to say, a multipoint measurement model needs to be developed.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks are so good now that almost nothing is lost, so the old way of injecting test packets to measure loss no longer gives a useful answer. Operators want to measure the traffic people actually send, without the users having to do anything or even notice.

sections.title: What Loss and Delay Measurement Demand
sections.content:
Modern networks, if not oversubscribed, generally drop relatively few packets, so packet loss measurement is highly sensitive to the common demarcation of the exact set of packets to be measured for loss. Without some form of colouring or batch marking, such as that proposed in RFC 8321, it may not be possible to achieve the required accuracy in the loss measurement of customer data traffic. Thus, when accurate measurement of packet loss is required, it may be economically advantageous, or even a technical requirement, to include some form of marking in the packets to assign each packet to a particular counter for loss measurement purposes.

When this level of accuracy is required and the traffic between a source and destination pair is subject to Equal-Cost Multipath, a demarcation mechanism is needed to group the packets into batches. Once a batch is correlated at both ingress and egress, the packet accounting mechanism can operate on the batch of packets that can be accounted for at both the packet ingress and the packet egress. Errors in the accounting are particularly acute in Label Switched Paths subjected to Equal-Cost Multipath, because the network transit time differs for the various paths since the packets may traverse different sets of Label Switching Routers, may depart from different interfaces on different line cards, and may arrive at different interfaces on different line cards.

A consideration with the solution of modifying the identity label, the MPLS label ordinarily used to identify the LSP, Virtual Private Network or Pseudowire, to indicate the batch is the impact this has on the path chosen by the Equal-Cost Multipath mechanism. When the member of the path set is chosen by deep packet inspection, a change of batch represented by a change of identity label has no impact on the path. If the path member is chosen by reference to an entropy label, then changing the batch identifier will not change the chosen path. Equal-Cost Multipath is so pervasive in multipoint-to-(multi)point networks that some method of avoiding the accounting errors it introduces needs to be supported.

On delay, most existing delay measurement methods are active methods that depend on an extra injected test packet to evaluate the delay of a path. With the active method, the rate, number and interval between the injected packets may affect the accuracy of the results. Due to Equal-Cost Multipath or link aggregation techniques, injected test packets may traverse different links from the ones used by the data traffic, so measuring the delay of the real traffic is required. For combined loss and delay measurements, both sets of considerations apply.
sections.plainLanguage: To count lost packets you have to know exactly which packets you were counting, and you have to count the same set at both ends. When traffic can take several equal-cost paths, the packets of one batch may take different routes and arrive at different times, which ruins the count.

sections.title: Four Things You Might Want to Identify
sections.content:
The most basic unit of identification is the identity of the node that processed the packet on its entry to the MPLS network. However, the required unit may vary depending on the use case for accounting, performance measurement or other types of packet observation, and there may be a need to impose identity at several different layers of the MPLS label stack. The document considers the identification of four traffic components: per source Label Switching Router, where everything from one source is aggregated; per group of LSPs chosen by an ingress router, where an ingress LSP aggregates a group of LSPs such as all the LSPs of a tunnel; per LSP, the basic form; and per flow within an LSP, a fine-grained method.

Note that a fine-grained identity resolution is needed when there is a need to perform these operations on a flow not readily identified by some other element in the label stack. Such a fine-grained resolution may be possible by deep packet inspection, but this may not always be possible, or it may be desired to minimise processing costs by doing this only on entry to the network. Adding a suitable identifier to the packet for reference by other network elements minimises the processing needed by other network elements. An example of such a fine-grained case might be traffic belonging to a certain service or from a specific source, particularly if matters related to service level agreement or application performance were being investigated.

The requirement can then be put in broad terms. There needs to be some way for an egress Label Switching Router to identify the ingress router with an appropriate degree of scope. There needs to be a way to identify a specific LSP at the egress node, which allows for the case of instrumenting multiple LSPs operating between the same pair of nodes, where the identity of the ingress router is insufficient. In order to conserve resources such as labels, counters and compute cycles, it may be desirable to identify an LSP group so that an operation can be performed on the group as an aggregate. And there needs to be a way to identify a flow within an LSP, which is necessary when investigating a specific flow that has been aggregated into an LSP.

The unit of identification and the method of determining which packets constitute a flow are specific to the application or use case and are out of scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: You might want to identify the traffic by where it entered the network, by which set of paths it is on, by one particular path, or by one particular flow within a path. Each is a different amount of work for the routers and gives a different amount of detail.

sections.title: Where the Existing Labels Are Enough
sections.content:
Several types of LSP have to be considered. The two simplest to monitor are point-to-point LSPs and point-to-multipoint LSPs. The ingress router for a point-to-point LSP, such as those created using RSVP-TE signalling or those that conform to the MPLS Transport Profile, may be identified by inspection of the top label in the stack, because at any provider-edge or provider router on the path the top label is unique to the ingress and egress pair at every hop at a given layer in the LSP hierarchy. Provided that Penultimate Hop Popping is disabled, the identity of the ingress router of a point-to-point LSP is available at the egress router, so determining the identity of the ingress router must be regarded as a solved problem. The identity of a flow, however, cannot be determined without further information being carried in the packet or gleaned from some aspect of the packet payload.

In the case of a point-to-multipoint LSP, and in the absence of Penultimate Hop Popping, the identity of the ingress router may also be inferred from the top label. However, it may not be possible to adequately identify the flow from the top label alone, so further information may need to be carried in the packet or gleaned from the payload. In designing any solution it is desirable that a common flow identification solution be used for both point-to-point and point-to-multipoint LSP types, and similarly that a common method of LSP group identification be used. In these cases a context label is needed to provide the required identity information, and this is a widely supported MPLS feature.

A more interesting case is the multipoint-to-point LSP. Here the same label is normally used by multiple ingress or upstream routers, so source identification is not possible by inspection of the top label by the egress routers, and it is therefore necessary for a packet to be able to explicitly convey any of the identity types described earlier. Similarly, in the case of a multipoint-to-multipoint LSP the same label is normally used by multiple ingress or upstream routers, so source identification is not possible by inspection of the top label, and the various identity types are again needed. The scope of the identity may, however, be constrained to be unique within the set of multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs terminating on any common node.
sections.plainLanguage: When one path carries the traffic, the label on the packet already says where it came from. When several sources share a path, the label no longer distinguishes them, so something extra has to be carried in the packet.

sections.title: What the Routers Can Cope With
sections.content:
There is a huge installed base of MPLS equipment; this type of equipment typically remains in service for an extended period, and in many cases hardware constraints mean it is not possible to upgrade its data-plane functionality. Changes to the MPLS data plane are therefore expensive to implement, add complexity to the network, and may significantly impact deployability. MPLS users have set a very high bar to changes to the data plane, and only a very small number have been adopted. It is important that the method of identification minimises changes to the MPLS data plane, and methods that require no changes should be given preferential consideration. If a method that changes the data plane is chosen, it needs a significant advantage over any method that makes no change, and that advantage needs to be carefully evaluated and documented. If a change is necessary, it should be as small a change as possible and a general-purpose method, so as to maximise its use for future applications, and it is imperative that any necessary change does not impose any foreseeable future limitation on the MPLS data plane.

Stack size is an issue with many MPLS implementations, both as a result of hardware limitations and because of the impact on networks and applications in which a large number of small payloads need to be transported. In particular, one MPLS payload may be carried inside another: one LSP may be carried over another LSP, or a Pseudowire or similar multiplexing construct may be carried over an LSP, and identification may be required at both layers. Of particular concern is the implementation of low-cost edge routers that, for cost reasons, have a significant limit on the number of label stack entries they can impose or dispose. Therefore any method of identity must not consume an excessive number of unique labels and must not result in an excessive increase in the size of the label stack.

The MPLS data plane provides two types of special-purpose labels: the original 16 reserved labels and the much larger set of special-purpose labels defined in a later document. The original reserved labels need one label stack entry, and the newer special-purpose labels need two. Given the tiny number of original reserved labels, it is core to the MPLS design philosophy that this scarce resource is only used when it is absolutely necessary. Using a special-purpose label to encode flow identity requires two label stack entries, one for the reserved label and one for the flow identity, and using extended special-purpose labels requires a total of three. The use of special-purpose labels as part of a method to encode identity information therefore has a number of undesirable implications for the data plane, so while a solution may use them, methods that do not require them need to be carefully considered.

On the control plane, any flow identity design should both seek to minimise the complexity of the control plane and minimise the amount of label coordination needed amongst routers. On backwards compatibility, it is unlikely that all routers will have the same capability to support the methods discussed, so it is an important constraint that any solution is backwards compatible with deployed equipment to the extent that deploying the new feature will not disable anything that currently works on legacy equipment. The design must support the coexistence of routers that can identify the traffic components described earlier and those that cannot, and the identification must be an optional feature that is disabled by default. As a design simplification, a solution may require that all egress routers of a point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint LSP support the identification type in use, so that a single packet can be correctly processed by all egress devices; the corollary is that either all egress routers are enabled to support the required identity type or none of them are.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a large installed base of routing gear that cannot be replaced, so any scheme has to work with the labels that already exist, or cost too much. The document sets out how little room there is to add new labels, and that the feature should be optional and off by default.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The inclusion of originating and flow information in a packet provides more identity information and hence potentially degrades the privacy of the communication. Recent IETF concerns on pervasive monitoring have resulted in a preference for a solution that does not degrade the privacy of user traffic below that of an MPLS network not implementing the flow identification feature. The choice of using MPLS technology for this OAM solution has a privacy advantage, as the choice of the label identifying a flow is limited to the scope of the MPLS domain and does not depend on the identification of the user data, which minimises the observability of the flow characteristics.

Any flow identification solution must not degrade the security of the MPLS network below that of an equivalent network not deploying the solution. In order to preserve present assumptions about MPLS privacy properties, propagation of identification information outside the MPLS network imposing it must be disabled by default. Any solution should provide for the restriction of the identity information to those components of the network that need to know it, so it is desirable to limit the knowledge of the identity of an endpoint to only those routers that need to participate in the traffic flow. The choice of using MPLS technology for this OAM solution, with MPLS encapsulation of user traffic, provides a key advantage over other data-plane solutions, as it provides for a controlled access and trusted domain within a service provider's network. For a more comprehensive discussion of MPLS security and attack mitigation techniques, the document points to the security framework for MPLS and GMPLS networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything that identifies traffic is a small loss of privacy, so the identity must stay inside the provider's network and must not travel outside it by default. Using the MPLS labels rather than looking inside the payload keeps that loss small.

viz.caption: The constraints any identification method has to respect

items.title: Change as little as possible
items.text: The data plane is expensive to change, so methods that need no change should be preferred.

items.title: Watch the label stack
items.text: A flow may be carried inside another flow, and low-cost edge routers have a limited number of label stack entries.

items.title: Reserved labels are scarce
items.text: There are only 16 original reserved labels, and they are meant to be used only when absolutely necessary.

items.title: Control plane too
items.text: A design should minimise both the complexity of the control plane and the label coordination needed between routers.

items.title: Optional and off by default
items.text: Routers that cannot identify the traffic must keep working, and the feature must be disabled unless it is wanted.
